text: [[@what-if-dinos-lived|When the big dinosaurs disappeared]], their "jobs" (big plant-eater, big hunter) were left empty. [[mammal|Mammals]] spread into those jobs. Over millions of years they became horses, elephants, bats, whales, monkeys and, eventually, humans.
This kind of change, where living things slowly change over many generations, is called [[evolution|evolution]]. [[@extinction|The asteroid]] didn't create mammals. It cleared the stage for them.

sec.t:
Mammals are almost as old as dinosaurs. The first ones appeared more than 200 million years ago, and for a very long time most stayed small, from shrew-sized to about the size of a cat.

Many were probably [[@nocturnal-animals|active at night]]. Small eyes, sharp [[@ears-hear|hearing]], a good sense of smell and warm, furry bodies helped them hunt insects in the dark, when big [[reptile|reptiles]] were less of a danger. Some scientists think this long night life is why many mammals today still [[@colour-blindness|see colours less well]] than birds and reptiles do.

They were not all timid. Repenomamus, from China, was about the size of a badger. One [[fossil|fossil]] has the bones of a young dinosaur inside its stomach.

For a long time, the fossil record from just after the disaster was patchy. Then, in 2019, a team working at Corral Bluffs near Colorado Springs described thousands of fossils from the first million years. They showed how fast things moved. Within a million years, some mammals weighed tens of kilograms, about as much as a big dog.

Much of this came from fossils hidden inside hard, rounded lumps of rock called concretions. For years, collectors had walked past them. Once the team learned what a lump with a skull inside looked like, they found them all over the hillsides. Teeth helped most of all. Mammal teeth are tough, so they fossilise well, and their bumps and ridges show whether an animal ate insects, seeds or leaves.

Plants changed alongside them. Early relatives of [[@pulses-dal|beans]] and walnuts appeared, giving mammals rich new foods. Bigger bodies and new foods seem to have gone together.

Over the next 20 million years, mammals spread into almost every way of life. Bats took to the air, the only mammals that can really fly. Some hoofed land mammals slowly returned to the water and became [[@whales-walked|whales]]. Early relatives of [[@elephants-talk|elephants]] grew in Africa, and India, then an island drifting north, had its own mammals.

Nothing did this on purpose. In each generation, the animals best suited to their surroundings left a few more young. Over enormous spans of time, small differences added up.

Primates, the group that includes [[@human-evolution|monkeys, apes and humans]], appear in the fossil record soon after the asteroid. Our own [[species|species]] turned up only about 300,000 years ago, in Africa. If the 66 million years since the asteroid were squeezed into one day, modern humans would arrive in the last seven minutes.

text: The Grand Canyon in [[@grand-canyon-state|Arizona]], USA, was carved by the Colorado River. Over millions of years, the river cut down through the rock while the land around it was slowly pushed upward. Sand and pebbles carried by the water worked like sandpaper.
Most [[geologist|geologists]] think the canyon took its shape in the last 5 to 6 million years, though parts may be older.

st.reveal: The Colorado River cut down through the rock, a little at a time, while the land around it was slowly pushed upward.

n.certNote: Geologists agree the Colorado River carved it. Exactly when the carving began is still debated.

myth: The Grand Canyon is the deepest canyon in the world.

It is one of the most famous, but not the deepest. The Yarlung Tsangpo canyon in Tibet, cut by the river that becomes the Brahmaputra, is several kilometres deeper. So is the Kali Gandaki gorge in Nepal.

sec.t:
The canyon walls are made of [[@earth-weird-rainbow-mountains|layers, like pages in a book]]. Each layer is a different ancient world: a shallow sea, a sandy desert, a muddy coast. The [[sediment|sediment]] piled up and hardened into rock.

Near the rim is the Kaibab Limestone, about 270 million years old, full of [[fossil|fossil]] sea sponges and shells. Below it lies the pale Coconino Sandstone, made from desert dunes, where fossil footprints of small four-legged animals still march across the stone. Each layer lets geologists [[@ancient-env|read an ancient world]].

The rocks at the bottom are about 1.8 billion years old, about 40% of [[@earth-age|Earth's age]]. In some places, younger rocks sit right on top of much older ones with a gap of over a billion years between them, as if pages were torn out of the book. Geologists call it the Great Unconformity.

On its own, water is too soft to cut rock quickly. But the Colorado River once carried huge loads of sand, gravel and boulders, especially during spring floods from melting snow in the [[@rocky-mountains|Rocky Mountains]]. Those rolled and scraped along the riverbed, grinding it down.

At the same time, the whole region, called the Colorado Plateau, was being pushed upward by forces deep [[@inside-earth|inside Earth]]. As the land rose, the river kept cutting, like a saw held still while the wood is pushed up into it. Rain, frost and side streams then widened the canyon, which is up to about 29 km across.

Today the Glen Canyon Dam, upstream, traps much of that sand in a [[reservoir|reservoir]]. The river below runs clearer and colder than it used to. [[@dams-power|Dams]] bring water and electricity, but they change rivers too.

{{story:national-parks}}

Here geologists disagree. Many think the Colorado River found its present route only 5 to 6 million years ago and carved most of the canyon since. Others argue that parts of it were cut by older rivers as far back as 70 million years ago, and the modern river joined them together. Clues from minerals that record when rocks cooled near the surface point both ways, so the debate goes on.

[[@native-nations|Native American peoples]] have lived in and around the canyon for thousands of years. The Havasupai still live deep inside a side canyon, and their village of Supai is so remote that mail arrives by mule.

In 1869, a one-armed Civil War veteran named John Wesley Powell led the first known [[expedition|expedition]] down the river through the canyon, in wooden boats. The canyon became a US [[@national-parks|national park]] in 1919, and millions of people visit every year.

The same thing happens in India. As the [[@himalaya-form|Himalayas rise]], rivers like the [[@rivers-himalaya|Ganga and its sisters]] cut deep gorges through them.

India has a smaller canyon of its own at Gandikota in Andhra Pradesh. There, the Penna River has carved a steep red gorge beside an old stone fort. Visitors often call it the Grand Canyon of India.

text: American bison once filled the grasslands of North America in herds so big they took days to pass. In the 1800s they were shot in huge numbers, for skins, for sport, and to push out the Native American nations who depended on them. By 1889, only about a thousand were left.

A few people, ranchers and Native American tribes saved small groups. Yellowstone [[@national-parks|National Park]] protected the last wild herd. Today there are again hundreds of thousands of bison, though most live on ranches, not in the wild.

Stand next to your outline. Then mark a wild water buffalo or a gaur, India's own giant cattle, from a library book or encyclopedia to compare.
myth: Bison are slow, gentle cows that are safe to walk up to.

Bison are wild and unpredictable. They can sprint at about 55 km/h and turn quickly. Every year a few visitors in Yellowstone are hurt after getting too close, so park rules say to stay at least 23 metres away.

sec.t:
For thousands of years, bison were the centre of life for nations of the Great Plains such as the Lakota, Cheyenne, Blackfeet and Comanche. Hunters used nearly every part of the animal. Meat was eaten fresh or dried. Hides became tipis, robes and shields. Bones became tools, and sinews became bowstrings and thread. Bison appear in their songs, ceremonies and stories, and many people still see them as relatives.

Nobody counted the herds properly. Estimates for how many bison lived around 1800 range from about 30 to 60 million.

In Yellowstone, poachers kept shooting the last wild herd. By 1902 only a couple of dozen remained there. The US Army, which then guarded the park, caught poachers, and a law in 1894 made killing wildlife in the park a crime. The park also brought in bison from private ranches to build up the herd.

Meanwhile, a handful of ranchers and Native American families had kept small groups alive. In 1905, Hornaday and others founded the American Bison Society. Two years later, the Bronx Zoo in New York sent 15 bison by train to a new wildlife refuge in Oklahoma. It was one of the first times a [[@zoos-sanctuaries|zoo]] helped return an animal to the wild.

Bison graze, roll in dust and trample the [[@soil-made|soil]]. This helps many plants, birds and insects. Their rolling leaves shallow hollows called wallows, which fill with rainwater and become tiny ponds for frogs and insects. Their grazing keeps grasses short in some patches and lets wildflowers grow.

Some tribes are bringing bison back to their lands to restore the prairie. The InterTribal Buffalo Council, formed in the early 1990s, now links dozens of tribes that keep herds of their own. Yellowstone sends some of its bison to tribal lands each year.

sec.h: Back from the brink in India
sec.t:
In 2016, the bison became the national [[mammal|mammal]] of the USA. It joined the [[@bald-eagle|bald eagle]], another animal saved from near extinction.

India has its own comeback stories, such as tigers after Project Tiger and the return of the [[@cheetah-return|cheetah]]. Its own giant wild cattle, [[@wild-indian-gaur|the gaur]], still roam forests in the Western Ghats and central India. Like the bison, they show that big animals can recover if they are given room and protection.

text: Chocolate comes from the seeds of the cacao tree. Its pods grow right out of the trunk and branches. Inside each pod are about 30 to 50 seeds, cocoa beans, wrapped in sweet white pulp.
Farmers let the beans ferment, dry them in the sun, then roast and grind them. Add sugar and milk, and you have chocolate.
The tree's scientific name, *Theobroma*, means "food of the gods" in Greek. It was given by the Swedish scientist Carl Linnaeus in the 1700s.

sec.h: A tree that flowers on its trunk
sec.t:
Cacao is a small tree that grows in the shade of taller rainforest trees. Unlike most trees, it grows its tiny white and pink flowers straight from the trunk and thick branches. A tree can produce thousands of flowers a year, but only a few out of every hundred become pods.

The pods are about the size of a papaya and turn yellow, orange, red or purple when ripe. Farmers cut them down with long-handled knives, crack them open and scoop out the slimy seeds.

People in Central America were drinking cacao thousands of years ago. [[@myths-maya|The Maya]] and Aztecs made a bitter, spicy, frothy drink. Cacao beans were so valuable the Aztecs used them as [[@money-worth|money]].

The tree's story may begin even earlier, further south. In 2018, scientists found traces of cacao in pots about 5,300 years old in Ecuador, in the upper Amazon. The [[@aztecs-maya|Maya]] later painted cacao pods on their [[@pottery|pottery]] and carved them on temples. They poured the drink from one cup to another, held high, to build up a thick foam.

In the 1500s, Spanish travellers brought cacao to Europe. There people added sugar and drank it hot. Solid chocolate bars came much later, in the 1800s.

{{story:chocolate-making}}

The fresh seeds are piled in heaps or boxes and covered with [[@bananas|banana]] leaves for about a week. [[yeast|Yeasts]] and [[bacteria|bacteria]] feed on the sweet pulp, warming the heap and starting the [[@fermentation|fermentation]] that turns the seeds brown and creates the first hints of chocolate flavour. Then the beans are spread out to dry in the sun.

Factories roast and crack the beans and grind the inside into a thick paste. In 1875, Daniel Peter in [[@switzerland|Switzerland]] mixed it with condensed milk to make the first milk chocolate. In 1900, Milton Hershey began selling chocolate bars in the USA, and a whole town in Pennsylvania grew up around his factory.

Cacao flowers are pollinated by tiny flies called midges. Like [[@fig-wasps|figs and their wasps]], the tree depends on a very small partner. Midges breed in rotting leaves and damp places on the forest floor, so farms with a bit of mess and shade often grow more pods than very tidy ones.

Cacao only grows in warm, wet places near the [[equator|equator]]. Most of the world's cocoa now comes from West Africa. Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana together grow more than half of it, mostly on small family farms. Investigations have found children doing hard and risky work on some of these farms, and chocolate companies and governments are under pressure to stop it.

India grows it too, mostly in Kerala, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu. There, cacao is often planted in the shade of coconut and areca palms, as a second crop for farmers.

One warning for pet owners: chocolate contains a chemical called theobromine, which humans handle easily but dogs can't. Even a small amount can make a dog seriously ill.

text: Your body is made of about 30 trillion [[cell|cells]], and lives with even more tiny [[bacteria|bacteria]], mostly in your gut. A 2016 estimate put the bacteria at about 38 trillion, a little more than your own cells.

Different cells do different jobs: nerve cells carry messages, red blood cells carry oxygen. [[@muscles|Muscle]] cells pull, skin cells protect, and fat cells store energy. There are a few hundred different kinds.
Cells are built from [[atom|atoms]], many of which were made in stars long ago.

steps.d: Your body has organs that do jobs: heart, lungs, brain, stomach.
Every organ is built from tiny living cells. You have around 30 trillion.
Inside most cells is DNA, the instruction book. Unwound, each cell's DNA is about 2 metres long!

myth: Every cell in your body is replaced every seven years, so you become a completely new person.

Different cells are replaced at very different speeds. Some gut cells last only days, red blood cells about four months, and many brain cells stay with you for life. There's no single seven-year cycle.

sec.t:
Each cell is a little bag of watery jelly wrapped in a thin skin called a membrane. Inside, thousands of tiny machines are at work. Some turn food into energy. Some build [[protein|proteins]], the materials your body is made from. Others carry things around or break down waste.

In most cells, a central control room called the [[nucleus|nucleus]] holds your [[@dna|DNA]]. That's the instruction book that tells the cell what to build and when. Every one of your cells started from the same instructions, copied from one single cell: the fertilised egg you grew from.

So why is a skin cell different from a brain cell if they carry the same book? Each kind of cell reads only some pages and keeps the rest closed. A muscle cell reads the pages for pulling, and a young red blood cell reads the pages for making the protein that carries oxygen.

By count, the most common cells in your body are [[@blood|red blood cells]]. A 2016 study by scientists in Israel worked out that they make up about 84% of all your cells. They're so small that a single drop of blood holds millions of them.

Other cells are far bigger. A human egg cell is just large enough to see without a [[microscope|microscope]]. Some nerve cells are the longest, stretching from the bottom of your spine to your toes, about a metre in a tall adult.

Your body replaces huge numbers of cells every day. Cells lining your gut last only a few days before they're worn out. Skin cells flake away and are replaced from below. Red blood cells last about four months.

Some cells hardly change at all. Many nerve cells in your brain and the cells in the lenses of your eyes stay with you for life. So the idea that you become a completely new person every seven years isn't true.

Cells team up. A group of similar cells forms a tissue, such as muscle. Tissues join to make organs, like your [[@heart-beat|heart]]. Organs work together in systems, like the heart and blood vessels moving blood around.

All of it is built from the same few kinds of atoms: mostly oxygen, carbon, hydrogen and nitrogen. Apart from hydrogen, nearly all of those atoms were made inside ancient [[@stars-born|stars]], which scattered them into space when they died, long before the Sun was born. Every time you breathe, you're using star leftovers.

text: An umbrella keeps you dry in two ways. First, its dome shape sends rain sliding off the edge and away from your head. Second, its cloth is woven so tightly, and coated so well, that raindrops can't find a way through.

Most umbrellas today use polyester or nylon threads woven into a tight cloth. Even so, there are tiny gaps between the threads. Raindrops stay out because of [[surface-tension|surface tension]]: water clings to itself like a stretchy skin, so a drop would rather stay round than squeeze through a tiny hole.

st.prompt: Rub your finger on the inside of a wet umbrella and water starts to drip through. Why?

options.t: Your finger breaks the water's surface skin and pushes it through the gaps
Your finger tears tiny holes in the cloth
The heat of your skin melts the coating

st.reveal: Water drops hold together with surface tension, a kind of stretchy skin. On their own they are too big to squeeze through the gaps in the weave. Touching the cloth from inside breaks that skin and gives the water a path through.

myth: Umbrellas were invented to keep off the rain.

sec.t:
The cloth is also treated with a coating that makes water bead up instead of soaking in. You can see this on a new umbrella: drops sit in little balls and roll away when you shake it. Leaves of the [[@lotus|lotus]] plant do the same trick naturally, which is why scientists study them to design better waterproof materials. The leaf is covered in tiny wax bumps, so a drop touches only their tips and can't spread out.

A coating like this is called water-repellent. Over years of use it wears off. That is why an old umbrella starts to let in a fine mist during heavy rain, even when there are no holes in it.

sec.h: The man who was laughed at
sec.t:
In Europe, umbrellas were long seen as something only women used against the sun. In the 1750s, a London traveller named Jonas Hanway began carrying one in the rain. People jeered at him in the street, and carriage drivers, who earned money from people escaping the rain, were especially rude. Within a few decades, umbrellas were common in London.

In the 1850s, a British maker named Samuel Fox introduced light steel ribs, which replaced heavy whalebone and cane. In the late 1920s, a German inventor patented a small umbrella that folded down short enough to carry in a bag.

An umbrella frame is a clever set of [[lever|levers]]. The long ribs hold the cloth. Shorter stretchers connect the ribs to a sliding ring on the shaft. When you push the ring up, the stretchers push the ribs outward and the cloth goes tight. A small spring catch holds it there. Many umbrellas have eight ribs, a number that balances strength against weight. Automatic umbrellas add a spring inside the shaft that pushes the ring up when you press a button.

A strong gust of [[@wind-blows|wind]] can get underneath and push the ribs the wrong way, flipping the umbrella inside out. Some modern designs have vents that let air escape, or bendy ribs made of fibreglass that spring back instead of snapping.

In Kerala, where the [[@monsoon|monsoon]] arrives first each June, umbrella-making is a big local industry, and many families buy new ones before the rains begin. Across India you see huge black umbrellas held by farmers, colourful folding ones in school bags, and giant beach umbrellas over fruit sellers' carts. It is one of the few inventions that is used in exactly the same way, for both sun and rain, all over the world.

text: Bandhani is a kind of tie-dye from Gujarat and Rajasthan. Artisans pinch up tiny points of cloth and tie each one tightly with thread. When the cloth is dipped in dye, the tied spots stay their original colour. The result is a pattern of small dots, sometimes forming flowers, birds, dancers or waves.
The word comes from *bandh*, meaning "to tie". It is one of India's oldest dyeing arts. A fine bandhani saree or dupatta can take weeks, because every dot is tied by hand.

st.prompt: In bandhani, why do the tied spots stay pale while the rest of the cloth changes colour?

options.t: The tight thread stops dye soaking into those spots
The spots are bleached afterwards
The spots are painted white at the end

st.reveal: Each tiny bundle of cloth is wrapped so tightly with thread that dye can't reach inside. When the threads are pulled off, the hidden dots show the cloth's earlier colour.

src: Development Commissioner (Handicrafts), Ministry of Textiles, Government of India, Bandhani of Gujarat and Rajasthan.

Real bandhani is tied by hand, knot by knot, and dyed by hand. Printed copies look flat, while true bandhani cloth has a slightly crinkled feel from all the knots.

sec.t:
First, a designer marks the pattern on the cloth, often by stamping it with a wooden block dipped in a colour that washes away. Then the tiers take over. Most are women, working at home in villages around Kutch and Jamnagar.

They pinch up a tiny point of cloth, wrap it several times with thread and move on to the next, without cutting the thread. Some grow a fingernail long or wear a small pointed metal ring to lift the cloth. Fine pieces have dots smaller than a grain of rice. A single dupatta can have thousands of knots. Some experts can tie hundreds in an hour.

sec.h: Light to dark, step by step

sec.t:
Bandhani is old. In the cave paintings at Ajanta, painted around 1,500 years ago, some figures wear clothes with dotted patterns that look like bandhani. Tie-dye of different kinds also grew up in Japan, where it is called *shibori*, and in West Africa, Indonesia and Peru.

In Gujarat and Rajasthan, the Khatri community has been known for bandhani for generations. Families pass down patterns and colour recipes from parents to children. Traditional dyes came from plants and minerals, such as madder for red, indigo for blue and pomegranate rind for yellow. Many dyers now use synthetic dyes, which are cheaper and brighter.

Bandhani colours often carry meaning. Red is linked with weddings and good luck. A Gujarati bride may wear a *gharchola*, a red and white bandhani saree with a grid of gold threads. Yellow is linked with spring and new beginnings, and some families give a yellow and red bandhani to a new mother.

In Rajasthan, a related style called *leheriya* makes wavy stripes instead of dots. The cloth is rolled diagonally, then tied at intervals before dyeing. It is especially popular during the [[monsoon|monsoon]] festival of Teej.

In the 1960s, tie-dye became hugely popular in the USA, on T-shirts with swirls of bright colour. The idea is the same as bandhani, even if the patterns are bolder and looser. Dye recipes, from yellow [[@turmeric|turmeric]] to deep indigo, are a story of kitchen science and trade. And if you want to see how two dye colours combine on cloth, [[@colour-mix|colour mixing]] explains why yellow under blue turns green. Across Gujarat, bandhani is just one of the many [[@india-wonder-kutch-crafts|Kutch crafts]] that fill village homes with colour.

text: Chikankari is a style of hand [[embroidery|embroidery]] from Lucknow, in Uttar Pradesh. Traditionally, embroiderers sew white cotton thread onto very fine, almost see-through white cloth. The patterns are vines, flowers, paisleys and leaves, built from dozens of different stitches.

What makes chikan special is its delicacy. Some stitches pull the threads of the cloth apart to make tiny holes like a net. Others are sewn from the back so the design glows softly through. A finished kurta looks light and cool, perfect for Lucknow's hot summers.

st.prompt: In the bakhiya stitch, the most famous chikankari stitch, where does the embroiderer sew?

options.t: On the back of the cloth, so the colour shows through as a shadow
Only along the edges
On top, using thick wool

st.reveal: In bakhiya, threads cross back and forth on the reverse side. From the front, you see a soft shadowy shape outlined by tiny stitches. It is often called shadow work for exactly that reason.

myth: Chikankari is always done by machine now.
Cheap machine copies are everywhere, but the real craft is still stitched by hand, mostly by women working at home in and around Lucknow. A single kurta can take days or weeks.

sec.t:
Making chikan is a team job. First a carver cuts flower patterns into wooden blocks. A printer dips the blocks in a blue dye and stamps the design onto the cloth. The dye is made to wash out, so it disappears once the stitching is done.

Next the cloth goes to the embroiderers, mostly women working from home in Lucknow and nearby villages. Many learnt from their mothers. Then comes washing, often by washermen who scrub the cloth to remove every trace of blue and [[starch|starch]] it for crispness. Finally it is ironed and sold. One fine kurta may pass through five or six pairs of hands.

A popular story says Nur Jahan, the wife of the Mughal emperor Jahangir, loved white embroidery and brought the art to India in the 1600s. It is a lovely tale, but there is no firm proof. White embroidery on fine cotton existed in Bengal and other places, and the craft probably grew from many influences.

What is certain is that chikan flourished in Lucknow under the Nawabs of Awadh in the 1700s and 1800s. They loved fine clothes, and Lucknow's craftspeople supplied them. In 2008, Lucknow chikan received a GI tag, so only work made in the Lucknow region can carry the name.

The first chikan was sewn on fine muslin, a cotton cloth so thin it was said to pass through a ring. Today it appears on cotton, silk, georgette and chiffon, in many colours besides white. Pastel shades and even bright colours are common.

Film costumes and designer weddings have made chikankari popular again. But most embroiderers are poorly paid, and machine-made copies sell for a fraction of the price. Groups in Lucknow now help women sell directly to buyers, so more of the money reaches the hands that did the work.

The love of light white clothes in hot places makes scientific sense. Pale cloth reflects sunlight, and thin cotton lets air move and [[@heat-body|sweat evaporate]]. Cotton itself has a long journey from fluffy boll to shirt, the story of [[@clothes-cotton|cotton]]. And Lucknow has another famous needle art, [[@art-zardozi|zardozi]], sewn with glittering metal thread fit for royalty.

text: Gothic cathedrals are the huge, pointed, window-filled churches built in Europe from the 1100s to the 1500s. Their builders used three clever tricks to go higher than anyone had before. Pointed arches sent the weight of the stone more steeply downwards. Ribbed vaults made the stone ceiling lighter. Flying [[buttress|buttresses]], stone arms on the outside of the building, held the walls up.

Together these let builders make walls thin, tall and full of stained glass. The result was a building that felt full of light and seemed to reach for the sky, which was exactly what its builders wanted.

st.prompt: What job do flying buttresses do on a Gothic cathedral?

options.t: They push back against the outward push of the heavy stone roof
They hold up the bells
They carry rainwater from the roof

st.reveal: A stone vault pushes outwards as well as down, which could make tall walls topple. Flying buttresses are stone arms that lean against the walls from outside, carrying that push down to the ground. With them, walls could be thinner and full of windows.

Some did collapse, like part of Beauvais Cathedral in 1284. But builders learned from experience and used careful geometry, and many cathedrals have stood for 700 or 800 years.

sec.t:
Stone is very strong when you squash it, but it cracks if it bends or gets pulled. A stone roof is heavy, and as [[@gravity-fall|gravity]] pulls it down, it also pushes the walls outwards.

Before Gothic, builders used round arches and very thick walls to hold that push. Churches in this older style, called Romanesque, were solid but dark inside, because big windows would weaken the walls.

With the buttresses doing the work outside, walls no longer needed to be thick. Builders filled them with huge windows of stained [[@glass-made|glass]], coloured with metals melted into the glass. Small pieces were held together with strips of lead to form pictures of saints and Bible stories.

Most people at the time could not read, so the windows taught stories in pictures. On a sunny day, coloured light spills across the stone floor. Chartres Cathedral in France still has most of its original glass from the 1200s.

There were no cranes with engines. Workers lifted stones with wooden cranes, sometimes powered by people walking inside a giant wheel, like a hamster wheel. Masons learned by apprenticeship and used compasses, string and simple [[geometry|geometry]] rather than written calculations.

A cathedral often took generations. Many workers never saw the one they worked on finished. Cologne Cathedral was started in 1248, paused for centuries, and only completed in 1880. Its spires, about 157 metres tall, made it briefly the tallest building in the world.

Builders sometimes pushed too far. At Beauvais in France, the stone vault over the choir reached about 48 metres, the highest ever built in the Gothic style. In 1284 part of it collapsed. It was rebuilt with extra supports, and the building was never completed as planned.

In 2019 a fire destroyed the roof and spire of Notre-Dame in [[@paris|Paris]]. Its stone vaults mostly held, protecting the inside. After five years of work by carpenters, stonemasons and glassmakers using many traditional methods, it reopened in December 2024.

The Gothic style spread across the world. In [[@mumbai|Mumbai]], the Victoria Terminus railway station, now Chhatrapati [[@shivaji|Shivaji]] Maharaj Terminus, mixes Gothic arches with Indian domes and carvings. In the United States, Washington National Cathedral was built in Gothic style over 83 years, finally completed in 1990. Even early [[@skyscrapers|skyscrapers]], with their pointed tops, borrowed Gothic ideas.

text: An entrepreneur is someone who starts a new business, taking a risk in the hope that it will succeed. The word comes from the French *entreprendre*, meaning "to undertake". Entrepreneurs spot a problem or a need, come up with a way to solve it, and gather the people, money and tools to make it happen.

A startup is a young company trying to grow fast, often using new technology. But entrepreneurs are everywhere: the woman who opens a tiffin service from her kitchen, the farmer who starts selling honey online, the teenager who fixes phones. What they share is a willingness to try something without knowing whether it will work.

st.reveal: The investor Aileen Lee coined the word in 2013, choosing a mythical animal because such companies seemed so rare. Today there are hundreds of them around the world, including dozens in India.

d.try: Think of a small problem at home or school, like lost pencils or a messy shoe rack. Sketch three possible fixes, then ask five people which one they would use and why. Change your best idea using what they said. That loop of trying, asking and improving is what entrepreneurs do every day.
myth: Successful entrepreneurs are lone geniuses who get it right first time.
Most businesses are built by teams, and most founders fail or change direction several times. Learning quickly from mistakes matters more than having a perfect first idea.

sec.t:
Running a startup is less about one brilliant idea and more about solving hundreds of small problems. Founders talk to customers, build a first simple version, see what goes wrong and improve it. They hire people, manage money and keep going when things fail.

Many startups need more money than the founders have. They may borrow, or they may sell part of their company to investors in return for cash. Some investors, called venture capitalists, put money into many young firms, knowing most will fail but hoping one or two will grow huge. Later, a successful company may sell shares on the [[@stock-market|stock market]].

India now has one of the largest startup scenes in the world. The government launched its Startup India programme in January 2016, offering tax breaks and simpler rules. By 2025, more than 1.5 lakh startups had been officially recognised.

Take Flipkart. In 2007, two former engineers, Sachin Bansal and Binny Bansal (who are not related), began selling books online from a small flat in Bengaluru. They sometimes delivered parcels themselves. Within about a decade it had grown into one of India's biggest online shops, selling everything from phones to fridges.

[[@indian-startups|Indian startups]] have changed how people pay, travel, shop and order food. Paying a shopkeeper with a phone, or booking an autorickshaw from an app, would have seemed odd to most people in 2010. Many new firms also come from smaller cities, not just Bengaluru, Delhi and Mumbai.

sec.h: Failure as part of the story
sec.t:
Most new businesses don't last. Estimates vary, but a large share of startups close within their first few years. Many entrepreneurs fail at least once before something works.

That isn't always a disaster. A failed startup teaches lessons and often leaves behind skilled people who start again. Some entrepreneurs aren't after money at all. Social entrepreneurs try to solve problems like clean water or education, sometimes as [[@cooperatives|cooperatives]] or charities. What counts, in the end, is whether people's lives get easier.

text: India became a hockey superpower in the late 1920s. A team of skilled players, led by the legendary [[@dhyan-chand|Dhyan Chand]], won the Olympic gold in Amsterdam in 1928. India then won every Olympic hockey gold until 1956, six in a row, and two more in 1964 and 1980.

Indian teams of that era played on grass with dazzling close control. Opponents often said the ball seemed glued to their sticks. When the sport moved to artificial turf in the 1970s, India struggled for decades. In recent years it has climbed back, winning Olympic bronze medals in Tokyo and Paris.

st.prompt: In the 1970s, a big change to the playing surface made it harder for India to keep winning. What was it?

options.t: Top matches moved from grass to artificial turf
The ball was made twice as heavy
Teams were cut from 11 to 7 players

st.reveal: Artificial turf, first used at the Olympics in 1976, made the ball run faster and favoured fitness and power over close dribbling skills. India also had very few turf pitches to train on.

d.try: Roll a marble or small ball across a carpet, then across a smooth tiled floor, pushing it with the same force each time. Measure how far it goes. Hockey teams faced exactly this change when they moved from grass to turf.
myth: Hockey is India's official national game.
Many textbooks and quiz books say so, but in 2012 the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports said in reply to a question that India has not declared any sport its national game.

sec.t:
Modern field hockey was organised in England in the 1800s, and British soldiers brought it to India. The first Indian clubs formed in Calcutta in the 1880s. Indian players took to it fast, especially in Punjab, the Bombay region and among army regiments.

The Indian Hockey Federation was formed in 1925. Three years later, India sent its first Olympic hockey team to Amsterdam. It won all five matches without conceding a goal and took gold.

The 1940 and 1944 Olympics were cancelled because of the [[@world-war-two|Second World War]]. When the Games returned in London in 1948, India played as an independent country for the first time. In the final, it beat Great Britain 4–0 at Wembley. For players who had grown up under British rule, it was a deeply emotional win.

India won again in 1952 and 1956. Pakistan, whose team grew from the same hockey traditions, beat India in the 1960 final, and the two neighbours became fierce rivals. India also won the men's World Cup in 1975, beating Pakistan 2–1 in the final in Kuala Lumpur.

In 1976 the Montreal [[@olympics|Olympics]] used artificial turf for hockey for the first time. On grass, bumps and long blades slow the ball. On the smooth carpet of plastic, with much less [[@friction|friction]], the ball zips along at speed. The game became faster and more physical, and fitness mattered as much as fine stick work.

Turf pitches were expensive, and India had only a handful. European and Australian teams trained on them every day. India's last Olympic gold for many years came in 1980, at Games where many top teams stayed away.

Change came slowly. Better coaching, more turf pitches and sponsorship helped. In 2018 the state of Odisha began sponsoring India's national hockey teams, and later built a large new stadium in Rourkela for the 2023 World Cup.

At the Tokyo Olympics, held in 2021, India's men beat Germany 5–4 to win bronze, their first Olympic medal in 41 years. The women's team finished fourth, their best ever result. In Paris in 2024 the men won bronze again, and Indian fans had a reason to cheer [[@olympics-india|Olympic]] hockey once more.

text: Kabaddi is a contact sport for two teams of seven players. One team sends a single player, the raider, across the middle line into the other team's half. The raider tries to touch as many defenders as possible and get back to their own half. The defenders try to grab and hold the raider so that they cannot get back.
Every defender the raider touches is out, if the raider gets home. If the defenders stop the raider, the raider is out. Teams take turns raiding, and the team with more points at the end wins.

st.prompt: In traditional kabaddi, how did the referee know a raider had not taken a fresh breath?

options.t: The raider had to keep chanting "kabaddi, kabaddi" without stopping
The raider had to keep his mouth shut
The referee watched the raider's chest

st.reveal: The chant, called the cant, proved the raider was still on one breath. If it stopped, he was out. Modern professional kabaddi uses a 30-second raid clock instead, though raiders still chant.

d.try: In a safe open space, mark a line with chalk or a rope. Take turns crossing it while saying "kabaddi, kabaddi" on one breath, then return. Count how long you can chant comfortably, but stop and breathe as soon as you need to.
myth: Kabaddi has been an official Olympic sport.
It has never been one. It was shown at Berlin in 1936 as a demonstration only. Its big international stage is the Asian Games, where it has been a medal sport since 1990.

sec.t:
Defenders work together. They often hold hands in pairs or chains and wait for the raider to come close, then pounce by grabbing an ankle or wrapping the raider's waist. A single defender diving at a raider risks being touched and sent off.

Out players can come back. When a team gets one of the other side out, one of its own out players returns. If a team loses all seven players, the opponents score two bonus points for an "all-out", and the whole team comes back on. The game swings in an instant, because a single raid can win or lose four or five points. Good raiders have lightning [[@reflexes|reflexes]] and can twist out of a grip in a split second.

Kabaddi has been played for centuries in villages across India and its neighbours, under many names. It is hu-tu-tu in parts of Maharashtra, chedugudu in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, and hadudu in [[@bangladesh|Bangladesh]], where it is the national sport. Iran, Pakistan, Nepal and South Korea have strong teams too.

The game needs no equipment at all. A flat patch of earth and some lines scratched with a stick are enough.

In 1936 members of the Hanuman Vyayam Prasarak Mandal, a sports club from Amravati, travelled to the Berlin [[@olympics|Olympics]] and demonstrated kabaddi and other Indian games. Kabaddi was standardised in the decades after independence.

It became a medal sport at the 1990 Asian Games in Beijing. India's men won every gold until 2018, when Iran beat them in the semi-final and went on to win. India took both the men's and women's golds back at the next Asian Games, held in 2023.

In 2014 a professional league, [[@kabaddi-league|Pro Kabaddi]], began, borrowing ideas from cricket's [[@ipl|IPL]]. It moved games indoors onto colourful mats, added the raid clock and put matches on prime-time television. Its first season drew huge audiences, and village players became household names.

Kabaddi is the closest cousin of [[@kho-kho|kho-kho]], India's other great chasing game. Both reward speed and teamwork. Kabaddi adds something extra: the courage to walk alone into a crowd of opponents and come back with points.

text: "The Flying Sikh" was Milkha Singh, one of India's greatest athletes. He was a 400-metre runner who won gold at the 1958 [[@commonwealth-games|Commonwealth Games]] and four Asian Games golds. At the 1960 Rome Olympics he came fourth, missing a medal by a fraction of a second. That race is still one of the most famous in Indian sport.
The nickname came from Pakistan, of all places. In 1960 he raced in Lahore and beat Pakistan's star sprinter. Pakistan's president, Ayub Khan, is said to have told him he had flown rather than run.

st.prompt: Who gave Milkha Singh the nickname "the Flying Sikh"?

options.t: Pakistan's leader, Ayub Khan, after a race in Lahore
India's prime minister, Jawaharlal Nehru
A British newspaper after the Commonwealth Games

st.reveal: In 1960 Milkha ran in Lahore against Pakistan's best sprinter, Abdul Khaliq, and won. Ayub Khan, then Pakistan's president, is said to have told him that he had not run, he had flown. The name stuck.

myth: Milkha Singh won a medal at the 1960 Olympics.
He came fourth in the 400 metres, just missing bronze. He later said he looked back at the other runners during the race, a mistake he regretted for the rest of his life.

sec.t:
Milkha Singh was born in Govindpura, a village in Punjab that became part of Pakistan in 1947. His exact birth date is unknown, but it was probably 1929. During the violence of [[@partition|Partition]], several members of his family were killed. He escaped to Delhi as a teenage [[refugee|refugee]], alone and frightened.

For a time he lived in refugee camps and struggled to survive. His elder brother encouraged him to join the army, which offered food, a uniform and a future. He was rejected three times before being accepted, around 1951 or 1952.

At the 1958 Commonwealth Games in Cardiff, Wales, Milkha won the 440 yards, beating South Africa's world-class runner Malcolm Spence. It was independent India's first gold medal at the Commonwealth Games. The same year he won the 200 metres and 400 metres at the Asian Games in Tokyo.

Prime Minister [[@nehru|Nehru]] asked what reward he wanted. Milkha asked for a national holiday, and one was declared.

In 1960 he was invited to race in Lahore, in the country where his family had died. He did not want to go, and agreed only after Nehru persuaded him. Huge crowds watched him beat Abdul Khaliq, Pakistan's fastest man. In 1962 he won two more Asian Games golds in Jakarta, in the 400 metres and the 4 × 400 metres relay.

At the 1960 Olympics in Rome, Milkha was one of the favourites for the 400 metres. In the final he started very fast, then eased slightly and glanced back. Three runners passed him. He finished fourth in about 45.6 seconds, a fraction behind the bronze medallist.

His time was a national record that lasted 38 years, until Paramjeet Singh broke it in 1998. Milkha later said that losing in Rome haunted him, and that he would give anything to see an Indian win an Olympic athletics medal.

Milkha married Nirmal Kaur, a former captain of India's women's volleyball team, and their son Jeev Milkha Singh became a top golfer. The family lived in [[@chandigarh|Chandigarh]]. In 2013 the film *Bhaag Milkha Bhaag* told his story to a new generation. He sold the film rights for one rupee.

He died in June 2021 from complications of COVID-19, a few days after his wife. Weeks later, [[@neeraj-chopra|Neeraj Chopra]] won javelin gold in Tokyo and dedicated it to him.

text: In para athletics, every event has a code made of a letter and a number. The letter tells you the kind of event: T for track, F for field. The number tells you the kind of impairment and how much it affects the sport.

Athletes with the same code compete against each other. So a race is never "everyone against everyone". It is runners whose bodies work in a similar way racing each other, and the best-trained one wins.

quiz.prompt: Two runners both have one leg missing below the knee. Which class would they most likely race in?

options.t: The same class, because their impairment affects running in a similar way
Different classes, because they come from different countries
Whichever class has fewer runners, so they win more easily

quiz.reveal: Classes are based on how an impairment affects the sport, not on country or luck. Two runners with similar leg impairments race together, so the fastest and best-trained athlete wins.

news.h: India wins a record 114 medals at the Asian Para Games in Japan
news.t: The Asian Para Games ended in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, on 24 October 2026. India won 114 medals, 30 gold, 35 silver and 49 bronze, beating its best from 2022 and finishing fourth, with para athletics alone bringing 65 medals. Every one of those races and throws was sorted by the class codes this entry explains.

d.try: Try throwing a soft ball as far as you can while standing, then while sitting on a chair. Measure both throws. Notice how much your legs help. Now you can see why seated throwers compete in their own class.
myth: Para athletes are not as serious about sport as other athletes.
Para athletes train for years, follow strict diets and break world records. Some para javelin throwers hurl it farther than many non-disabled club athletes.
facts: track events, like running and wheelchair racing
field events, like throwing and jumping
runners who are blind, racing with a guide
runners with a leg missing below the knee, on a blade

sec.t:
The first number shows the group. Numbers in the 10s are for athletes with a vision impairment, the 20s for an intellectual impairment, and the 30s to 60s for different physical impairments.

The second number shows how strongly the sport is affected. A lower number usually means a bigger effect. So a T11 runner is blind and races with a guide, while a T13 runner can see a little.

For example, T64 is for runners with a leg missing below the knee who race on a carbon-fibre [[@prosthetics|prosthetic]] blade. F57 is for throwers who compete sitting down, because legs give a big push to a [[@sport-science-javelin|javelin]] throw.

{{story:paralympics}}

Before competing, athletes are checked by trained experts called classifiers, usually doctors and coaches. They test strength, movement or sight, and watch the athlete do their sport, to [[classify|classify]] them correctly. An athlete can be checked again later if their body changes.

It is not perfect. Bodies are all different, and people still argue about where some lines should be drawn. But the aim is simple: win because you trained hardest, not because of your body.

The same system runs from the [[@paralympics|Paralympics]] to the Asian Para Games, a [[tournament|tournament]] that began in 2010 and are held soon after the [[@asian-games|Asian Games]]. India won 114 medals at the 2026 Games in Japan, its best ever, and many of its [[@sport-paralympians-india|para athletes]] are now household names.

Every class also sends a message about [[@disabilities-inclusion|inclusion]]: when the rules are fair, everyone can take part.

text: Indian children have played street and courtyard games for centuries, often with nothing more than a stick, a few stones or a chalk line. Some are team chasing games, like [[@kho-kho|kho-kho]] and [[@kabaddi|kabaddi]]. Others need a bit of gear: a stick and a wooden peg for gilli-danda, marbles for kancha, a spinning top called a lattu, or a stack of flat stones for lagori.

There are quieter games too. Board games like pachisi, chaupar and pallanguzhi were played on cloth, wood or floors scratched with chalk. Several Indian games travelled the world and came back as famous brands.

Pallanguzhi, popular in Tamil Nadu and Kerala, uses a wooden board with two rows of seven cups and a handful of seeds or shells. Players scoop and sow the seeds around the board, capturing as they go. It belongs to a family of counting games called mancala, played from Africa to Southeast Asia, and it quietly trains children to count and plan ahead.

sec.t:
About 1,500 years ago, Indian players moved pieces representing an army's four parts, elephants, chariots, horses and foot soldiers, across a board. The game was chaturanga. It travelled to Persia and then Europe and slowly became modern [[@chess-india|chess]].

Pachisi, played with cowrie shells as dice, travelled to England, where a simpler version was sold as Ludo from the 1890s. And gyan chaupar, also called mokshapat, became [[@snakes-ladders|snakes and ladders]]. In the old boards, ladders rose from good deeds and snakes dropped from bad ones.

Lagori goes by many names: pithoo in the north, lagori in Karnataka, satoliya in some places, seven stones in English. A team knocks over a pile of seven flat stones with a ball, then tries to rebuild it before being hit.

Kancha, or marbles, is played by flicking glass balls with a bent finger to strike others. Lattu are wooden tops wound with string and thrown so they spin on the ground. Good players can scoop a spinning lattu onto their palm. Stapu or kith-kith, a hopping game on chalk squares, is close to American hopscotch.

Most of these games cost almost nothing. A stick from a tree or a few stones from a lane is enough. Rules change from one street to the next, and children argue about them as fiercely as umpires.

The government's Khelo India programme now includes traditional sports like mallakhamb and kalaripayattu, and some schools teach old games again. Kids in other countries play cousins of the same games, from tag to marbles to hopscotch, which you can see in [[@life-games-playground|playground games]] around the world. Even the emperor [[@akbar|Akbar]] liked a good board game. At Fatehpur Sikri, a courtyard is laid out like a huge pachisi board, where he is said to have played using people as the pieces.

[[archaeologist|Archaeologists]] have found toys in ancient cities across the world. In the [[@indus-cities|Indus cities]], children had clay [[@whistles|whistles]] and carts. sec.t:
At Harappa, Mohenjo-daro and other Indus Valley sites, archaeologists have found hundreds of small clay objects that were almost certainly toys. There are miniature carts with wheels, clay animals such as bulls, monkeys and birds, and little whistles shaped like birds.

Some animals have heads that nod when a string is pulled. These toys are about 4,500 years old. They also help historians, because they show what the real carts and animals of the time looked like, and remind us that the [[@wheel-invented|wheel]] was used in India very early.

India has a long tradition of handmade toys, many made in particular towns. In Channapatna, near [[@bengaluru|Bengaluru]], craftspeople turn wood on a lathe and colour it with lacquer and natural dyes. [[@channapatna-toys|Channapatna toys]] have a Geographical Indication tag, which protects their name.

[[@art-toy-making-kondapalli|Kondapalli]] in Andhra Pradesh is famous for light wooden figures, and Etikoppaka for lacquered toys coloured with plant dyes. The Thanjavur dancing doll, or thalaiyatti bommai, has a weighted base and a head that sways. Children across India have also played with lattus, gilli-danda, [[@marbles-tops|marbles]] and [[@kite-flying|kites]].

In the 1800s, factories in Germany and elsewhere began making tin toys, train sets and [[@pop-barbie-dolls|porcelain dolls]] in large numbers. Toys became cheaper, but many families still made their own.

In 1902 a cartoon showed US President Theodore Roosevelt refusing to shoot a captured bear on a hunting trip. A shop owner in New York, Morris Michtom, made a stuffed bear and called it "[[@pop-teddy-bear|Teddy's bear]]". A German company, Steiff, was making toy bears at the same time, and teddy bears soon spread around the world.

After the [[@world-war-two|Second World War]], cheap [[@plastic-made|plastic]] changed toys again. [[@pop-lego-history|Building bricks]] like [[@lego|LEGO]], plastic dolls and action figures filled shops. Today children also play [[@video-games|video games]] and use apps.

Yet many of the oldest toys never went away. A ball, a top or a doll is still among the first toys many children own. Archaeologists say this tells us something about being human. Children everywhere, in every age, have found ways to play.

text: The coloured ring in your eye is called the iris. Its colour comes mainly from melanin, the same brown [[pigment|pigment]] that colours skin and hair. Lots of melanin makes brown eyes. Less makes hazel or green. Very little makes blue or grey.

Many babies are born before their irises have made much melanin. Over the first months of life, special cells in the iris start making more. So a baby born with blue-grey eyes may end up with green, hazel or brown eyes by around their first birthday. Sometimes the change carries on slowly until age three.
In India and across much of Asia and Africa, most babies are born with dark eyes, and they stay dark.

options.t: Babies born with dark brown eyes
Babies born with blue eyes

st.reveal: Dark brown eyes already have plenty of melanin at birth, so they usually stay brown. Light blue or grey eyes have little melanin yet, and in the months after birth they may darken to green, hazel or brown.

myth: Eye colour is decided by one gene, and brown always beats blue.
Many genes work together to set eye colour. That's why two blue-eyed parents can, rarely, have a child with brown or green eyes, and why there are so many in-between shades.

sec.t:
Here is the strange part. Blue eyes have no blue pigment at all. The front layer of a blue iris has very little [[melanin|melanin]]. When light enters it, tiny fibres scatter short, blue [[wavelength|wavelengths]] more than long, red ones. Some of that blue light bounces back out to someone looking at you.

It is the same effect that makes the [[@sky-blue|sky blue]]: air scatters blue sunlight more than red. Green eyes are a mix, with a little yellowish pigment plus scattered blue. Brown eyes have so much melanin that it soaks up most of the light, so they look brown in every lighting.

That's also why light eyes can seem to change shade with clothes, weather or lighting. The structure stays the same, but the light around them changes.

{{story:sky-blue}}

Melanin is made by cells called melanocytes. Before birth, in the darkness of the womb, these cells in the iris have little reason to work hard. After birth, light and the baby's growing body switch them on.

How much melanin they end up making depends on [[gene|genes]] from both parents. If the genes say "make a lot", the eyes darken quickly, maybe within weeks. If they say "make only a little", the eyes stay blue. Doctors usually say a baby's eye colour is fairly settled by about a year old.

Babies' eyes are changing in other ways too. A newborn sees mostly blurry shapes, best at about 20 to 30 cm, roughly the distance to a parent's face during feeding.

At school, you might hear that eye colour follows a simple rule: brown beats blue. Real life is messier. Scientists have found more than a dozen [[@genes-family|genes]] that affect eye colour, and some research points to many more.

Two of them, called OCA2 and HERC2, matter most. In 2008, scientists in Copenhagen reported that blue-eyed people seem to share one small change near the OCA2 gene. They suggested it first appeared in a single person who lived roughly 6,000 to 10,000 years ago.

About 70 to 80 per cent of people in the world have brown eyes. Blue eyes are common mainly in northern Europe. Green eyes are among the rarest, found in only a small slice of people worldwide.

A few people have eyes of two different colours, or one iris with two colours in it. This is called heterochromia. It is usually harmless and simply means melanin is spread unevenly. Huskies, cats and some horses often have it too.

If an older child or adult's eye colour suddenly changes, though, it is worth seeing a doctor, because it can sometimes be a sign of an eye problem. For babies, a slow change is normal and expected.

Melanin does more than colour eyes. It also decides the shade of your [[@skin-colour|skin]] and hair, and it shields your body from the Sun's [[ultraviolet|ultraviolet]] light. That's why people whose ancestors lived in sunny places tend to have darker skin and eyes.

text: Before you were born, you grew inside your mother for about nine months. You could not eat or breathe there, so everything you needed came through the umbilical cord, a soft tube connecting your tummy to the [[placenta|placenta]]. The placenta passed oxygen and food from your mother's blood into the cord, and carried waste away.

After birth, a baby can breathe and feed, so the cord is no longer needed. It is clamped and cut. That does not hurt, because the cord has no nerves. The little stump left behind dries up and falls off within a week or few. What remains is a scar: your belly button, or navel.

st.reveal: Doctors clamp and cut the cord in much the same way for every baby. Whether the scar sinks in or sticks out depends on how the body heals, and sometimes on a small bulge of tissue underneath.

sec.t:
Most people have an innie, a navel that dips inwards. Some have an outie, which sticks out. The shape depends on how the skin and the tissue under it healed after the stump came off. It has nothing to do with how the cord was cut.

Some babies have a small bulge at the navel called an umbilical hernia, where a bit of tissue pushes through a gap in the tummy muscles. It looks odd but usually closes by itself within the first few years.

Ever pulled a tiny ball of fluff from your navel? A chemist in Austria studied hundreds of samples and found it is mostly fibres from your clothes, mixed with dust, dead skin and sweat. Little hairs on your tummy act like a ratchet, scraping fibres off your shirt and pushing them towards the navel as you move.

People with hairier tummies tend to collect more. An Australian man spent years saving his own navel fluff and filled several jars, earning a world record for it.

Almost all [[mammal|mammals]] have belly buttons, because almost all of them grow inside their mothers attached to a placenta. Dogs, cats, cows and [[@dolphins-click|dolphins]] all have one, though fur often hides it and the scar is usually flat and thin.

Animals that hatch from eggs, like birds, crocodiles and turtles, are fed by a yolk inside the egg. They have a small yolk-sac scar for a while, but it usually fades. The odd one out is the [[@power-platypus|platypus]], a mammal that lays eggs, and it has no belly button at all.

Keeping your navel clean is easy: wash it in the shower or bath and dry it well. Deep innies can trap sweat and lint, which may smell if left for a long time. If a belly button becomes red, sore or leaks fluid, tell a parent or doctor.

For new babies, doctors and nurses usually advise keeping the cord stump clean and dry until it drops off by itself. The cord was only one part of a bigger story. In nine months, you grew from a single cell smaller than a full stop into a [[@baby-development|baby]] of about 3 kg, with every finger, eyelash and heartbeat in place.

text: Mosquitoes are dangerous because of what they carry. When a [[@mosquitoes-bite|female mosquito bites]] someone sick with certain diseases, she can pick up germs with the blood. When she bites the next person, she can pass them on.

That's how malaria, dengue, chikungunya, Zika, yellow fever, Japanese encephalitis and other diseases spread. Malaria alone killed about 600,000 people in 2023, according to the World Health Organization, most of them young children in Africa. [[@what-if-no-mosquitoes|Mosquitoes themselves are tiny and weak]]. It's their role as flying needles that makes them so deadly. Mosquito-borne diseases have even changed the course of [[@disease-history|history]], wrecking armies and halting canal-builders.

sec.t:
Female mosquitoes need [[protein|protein]] from blood to make their eggs. Male mosquitoes never bite. Both eat [[nectar|nectar]] and plant juices for energy.

A female finds you mainly by smell. She can sense the [[carbon-dioxide|carbon dioxide]] in your breath from several metres away, then homes in on body heat and skin chemicals. Some people really do get bitten more than others, probably because of the mix of chemicals on their skin.

Mosquitoes lay their eggs in water. The [[larva|larvae]] wriggle in puddles, ponds and containers for about a week before turning into flying adults. That's why mosquito numbers shoot up in the [[@monsoon|monsoon]], when every pothole, drain and forgotten bucket fills with rainwater.

Anopheles mosquitoes carry malaria. They mostly bite between dusk and dawn, which is why bed nets treated with insecticide save so many lives.

Aedes mosquitoes, with black-and-white striped legs, carry dengue, chikungunya, Zika and yellow fever. They bite during the day and breed in small amounts of clean, still water in pots, coolers, tyres and flower vases. Dengue cases rise in many Indian cities after the [[monsoon|monsoon]] each year. Culex mosquitoes spread Japanese encephalitis in Asia and West Nile virus, which reached the USA in 1999 and has since spread across the country.

The USA wiped out malaria in the early 1950s by draining swamps, spraying, using screens on windows and treating patients. India has cut malaria cases sharply in recent decades and aims to end it by 2030.

New tools are helping. In 2021, the WHO recommended the first malaria [[@vaccines|vaccine]] for children, and in 2023 a second one, R21, which is manufactured in India by the Serum Institute. Scientists are also releasing mosquitoes carrying [[bacteria|bacteria]] called Wolbachia, which stop them from spreading dengue well.

Simple steps still matter most: removing standing water, using nets and repellents, and wearing long sleeves at the times mosquitoes bite. Anyone who gets a high fever, especially during the monsoon, should see a doctor quickly.

text: The Bharatiya Antariksh Station, or BAS, is India's plan for its own space station: a home and laboratory circling Earth where Indian astronauts can live and work for weeks at a time. "Antariksh" means space in Hindi and Sanskrit.

India's Cabinet approved the first stage in September 2024. ISRO plans to launch the first module, BAS-1, in 2028, and to complete a five-module station by 2035. If it happens, India would join the USA, Russia and China as one of only a few countries to run a space station of its own.

sec.t:
A space station is too heavy to launch in one go. The plan is to send up five modules, one at a time, starting with ISRO's most powerful rocket today, the LVM3. Each one will be joined to the others while they [[orbit|orbit]] Earth at about 28,000 km per hour.

When finished, BAS should weigh around 52 tonnes and circle about 400–450 km above the ground. That is about as far up as Goa is from Mumbai along the coast. The [[@space-station|International Space Station]], which has been visited by astronauts from many countries since 2000, is much bigger, at about 420 tonnes. BAS is meant to be smaller, simpler and fully Indian-run.

In August 2025, ISRO showed a model of the first module at an exhibition in New Delhi for National Space Day. It was the first time the public could see what the station might look like.

A space station is a laboratory where [[gravity|gravity]] seems to vanish. Scientists call this [[microgravity|microgravity]]. In it, flames burn in round balls, water forms floating spheres and plants grow their roots in strange directions.

Indian astronauts on BAS are expected to study how the human body changes in space, test new materials and medicines, and grow plants. Long stays help doctors learn how to protect astronauts' bones and muscles, which weaken without gravity to work against. That knowledge matters for any future trip to the Moon or Mars.

Running a space station is hard and costly. Supplies, water and spare parts must be sent up regularly, and the crew must be brought home safely. Some people ask whether the money would be better spent on other things. Supporters argue that the station will train Indian scientists and engineers, build new industries, and let India carry out experiments on its own timetable.

The International Space Station is expected to be retired around 2030. After that, the main stations in orbit may be China's Tiangong, private stations being built by American companies, and, if all goes to plan, BAS.

ISRO began with small rockets launched from a church in Thumba, Kerala, in the 1960s, under [[@vikram-sarabhai|Vikram Sarabhai]]. Six decades later, it has landed on the Moon and is planning a home in orbit. Space projects often run late, and BAS may too. In January 2026, ISRO invited Indian companies to help build the first module, so the work has already moved from drawings to hardware.

text: Akbar was the third Mughal emperor. He ruled from 1556 to 1605, nearly 50 years, and turned a shaky kingdom into one of the strongest [[empire|empires]] in the world.

He is called "the Great" for several reasons. He conquered and organised a huge [[territory|territory]]. He made alliances with Hindu [[@rajputs|Rajput]] kings and gave them high posts. He set up a fairer, better-measured land tax. Most of all, he treated people of different religions with unusual respect for his time, abolishing a tax on non-Muslims and inviting scholars of many faiths to debate. His idea of *sulh-i-kul*, "peace with all", still sounds modern. But he could also be ruthless in war.

sec.t:
Akbar was born in 1542 in a desert fort in Sindh, while his father Humayun was on the run. In 1556, Humayun fell down the stairs of his library and died. Akbar, just 13, became emperor.

Within months, a general named Hemu captured [[@delhi|Delhi]]. At the Second Battle of Panipat, Hemu was hit in the eye by an arrow, his army scattered and Akbar's side won. For a few years, Akbar's guardian, Bairam Khan, ran the empire. Then the teenager took charge himself.

In 1575 Akbar built a hall at Fatehpur Sikri called the Ibadat Khana, the House of Worship. At first only Muslim scholars debated there. Later he invited Hindu pandits, Jain monks, Zoroastrian priests and [[@india-wonder-goa-history|Jesuit missionaries from Goa]].

Akbar listened to them all. He ordered books such as the [[@mahabharata|Mahabharata]] and [[@ramayana|Ramayana]] translated into Persian, with rich paintings. His Persian Mahabharata is called the *Razmnama*, the "Book of War". He seems to have believed that every religion held part of the truth.

Stories say Akbar had nine special courtiers, the *navratnas*. The list varies, but it usually includes Birbal, famous for his wit; Tansen, the great singer; Todar Mal, who organised the land tax; and Abul Fazl, who wrote Akbar's history.

Todar Mal's system measured fields and set [[@taxes|taxes]] based on average crops over ten years. Birbal was a real minister and friend of Akbar, though the funny stories about him were mostly made up later. Tansen's music shaped [[@carnatic-hindustani|Hindustani classical music]] for centuries.

Akbar never learned to read or write well, perhaps because he spent his childhood on the move. Yet he loved books and had them read aloud to him every day. His library held thousands of [[manuscript|manuscripts]].

He built a red sandstone city at Fatehpur Sikri, with a giant gateway called the Buland Darwaza. The court left it after about 14 years, possibly because of water shortages. Its empty palaces still stand, a UNESCO [[@unesco-sites|World Heritage]] Site near Agra.

text: The Industrial Revolution was a time, starting in Britain around 1760, when people began making things with machines in factories instead of by hand at home. Machines were powered first by water wheels and then by steam engines burning coal.

It began with [[@clothes-cotton|cotton cloth]] and spread to iron, coal, railways and much more. Goods became cheaper and more plentiful. Millions of people moved from villages to [[@cities-grow|fast-growing cities]] to work in factories. It also brought long hours, [[@child-labour|child labour]], smoky air and, in places like India, the collapse of old industries. Our world of [[@electricity-made|electricity]], cars and phones grew out of it.

st.prompt: In Britain's early cotton mills, many workers were children. What job were small children often given?

sec.t:
Britain had a lot of coal close to the surface, plenty of rivers to turn water wheels, and money from trade and its [[empire|empire]]. It also had inventors and business owners eager to try new ideas, and laws that protected inventions with [[@inventions-weird|patents]].

There was also demand. People in Britain wanted the light, colourful cotton cloth that came from India. Making it by hand in Britain was slow and expensive, so inventors tried to make machines do it.

Factories needed iron for machines and coal for fuel. Mines went deeper, and steam engines pumped water out of them. In 1825 the first public railway to use steam engines opened in northern England, and in 1830 a line linked Liverpool and Manchester. Within decades, railways crossed Britain, Europe and North America. In 1853, India's first passenger train ran 34 km from Bombay to Thane, beginning [[@indian-railways|India's railways]].

Manchester grew so fast from cotton that people nicknamed it "Cottonopolis". Workers, including many children, often worked 12 hours or more a day. Housing was crowded, and chimneys filled the air with soot.

Slowly, laws changed. Britain limited children's working hours in the 1830s and 1840s. Workers formed [[@unions|trade unions]]. Over time, more children went to school instead of to work.

India had been famous for its cotton cloth for centuries. Fine muslin from Dhaka and printed calico were sold across Asia, Africa and Europe.

Under British rule, India's raw cotton was shipped to Lancashire's mills, woven into cloth by machines, and sold back in India more cheaply than local weavers could match. Millions of handloom weavers lost their living. Historians still debate exactly how much damage this did, but it became one of the strongest complaints of the freedom movement. [[@khadi|Gandhi's khadi]], hand-spun and hand-woven cloth, was a direct answer to it.

India later built its own mills. The first cotton mill in Bombay opened in 1854, and the city became a great mill town. The first factories in the USA were cotton mills too, starting in New England in the 1790s.

text: The Kohinoor is a diamond of 105.6 carats, about the weight of seven one-rupee coins. It was probably mined in the Golconda region of south India, centuries ago. It passed between Mughal emperors, a Persian conqueror, Afghan rulers and Maharaja Ranjit Singh of Punjab. In 1849, after the British East India Company defeated the Sikh kingdom, it was taken and sent to Queen Victoria.

Today it sits in a crown in the Tower of London, where millions of visitors see it each year. India, Pakistan, Afghanistan and Iran have all claimed it at different times. The British government's position is that it was handed over legally under a [[treaty|treaty]]. Many people in South Asia see it as a symbol of [[colonial|colonial]] loot.

sec.h: A diamond with a misty past
sec.t:
Diamonds from [[@golconda|Golconda]], near today's Hyderabad, were famous across the world for centuries. These mines produced many legendary stones, and the Kohinoor was very likely one of them.

Its early story is hazy. The Mughal emperor Babur wrote about a huge diamond in 1526, and some historians think it was the Kohinoor. Others disagree. Legends say it was worn by gods or ancient kings, but there is no evidence for those stories. The first clear sighting comes from 1739, in Delhi.

Ranjit Singh died in 1839, and his kingdom fell into turmoil. After two wars with the [[@east-india-company|East India Company]], Punjab was taken over in 1849. A treaty forced the ten-year-old Maharaja Duleep Singh to give up the Kohinoor to the Queen of England.

The stone was shipped to Britain in 1850 and shown at the Great Exhibition in London in 1851. Crowds lined up, but many were let down. Uncut, it looked more like a lump of glass than a blaze of fire.

In 1852, Prince Albert, Queen Victoria's husband, had it recut to make it shine. The work took 38 days. The diamond shrank from about 186 carats to 105.6 carats, losing about 43% of its weight. It sparkled more, but some experts thought the cut was poor.

Since then it has been worn only by queens. It was set into the crown made for Queen Elizabeth, the Queen Mother, in 1937. At the coronation of King Charles III in 2023, Queen Camilla wore a different crown, a choice many people saw as a way to avoid controversy.

Since India's independence in 1947, Indian politicians and campaigners have asked for the diamond back several times. Pakistan, Afghanistan and Iran have also claimed it. Britain has always said no.

Both sides have serious arguments. Some point to the treaty. Others say a treaty forced on a defeated ten-year-old can't be fair. The question is part of a much bigger debate about objects taken in colonial times and kept in museums. For now, the mountain of light stays in the Jewel House, among the other [[@crown-jewels|crown jewels]], behind thick glass, glowing for tourists.

text: The Great Sphinx of Giza, a lion with a human head carved from a hill of limestone, has guarded the desert near the [[@pyramids|pyramids]] for about 4,500 years. Its nose, about 1 m wide, is missing.

For a long time, people liked to say that Napoleon's soldiers knocked it off with cannon fire. They didn't. A Danish traveller, Frederic Louis Norden, drew it without a nose in 1737, long before Napoleon came. Marks on the face show the nose was deliberately pried off with rods or chisels. The Egyptian historian al-Maqrizi, writing in the 1400s, said a man named Muhammad Sa'im al-Dahr damaged the face in 1378.

st.prompt: How do experts know the Sphinx's nose didn't just fall off from wind and weather?

options.t: They found marks from rods or chisels hammered into the face
They found the nose buried nearby
A carving on the paw explains what happened

st.reveal: Close study shows marks where long rods or chisels were driven in, near the nose and under it, to pry it away. That points to people breaking it off on purpose, not to wind or sand.

sec.h: A lion as long as a jumbo jet
sec.t:
The Sphinx is about 73 m long, about as long as a large passenger jet, and 20 m high, as tall as a six-storey building. Most experts think it was carved for the pharaoh Khafre, whose pyramid stands behind it. Its face may even be his portrait.

It wasn't built from blocks. Workers carved it out of the bedrock, cutting away the stone around it. The head is made of harder rock than the body, which is why the body has worn away more.

When new, the Sphinx was probably painted. Traces of red paint survive on its face. It wore a royal striped headcloth, and at some point gained a long, braided beard like the gods.

In 1798, [[@napoleon|Napoleon]] invaded Egypt with an army and also more than 150 scientists, artists and engineers. They measured and drew monuments, and their soldiers found the Rosetta Stone, which later helped scholars read [[@hieroglyphs|hieroglyphs]].

Because French soldiers were there with cannons, the story of them using the Sphinx for target practice was easy to believe. It still appears in films and cartoons. But Norden's drawing and other older pictures prove the nose was gone before 1798.

For much of its life, the Sphinx was buried up to its shoulders in sand. Around 3,400 years ago, a prince who later became the pharaoh Thutmose IV is said to have dozed beside it. In a dream, the Sphinx promised him the throne if he cleared the sand. He did, and set up a stone slab, the Dream Stele, between its paws. It's still there.

Later diggers cleared the sand again in the 1800s and 1920s. Pieces of the fallen beard were found and taken to the British Museum and to Cairo. Today, [[conservator|conservators]] patch crumbling stone on the body and watch out for groundwater, which can damage the limestone from below. Repairing old statues is a delicate job, and the experts behind [[@behind-art-restoration|art restoration]] argue about how much to fix.

text: The Rocky Mountains, or Rockies, are the great mountain range of western North America. They run for more than 4,800 kilometres, from northern British Columbia in Canada down through Montana, Wyoming and Colorado to New Mexico in the USA. Their highest peak is Mount Elbert in Colorado, at 4,401 metres.

Compared with the old, rounded [[@appalachians|Appalachians]] in the east, the Rockies are young and jagged. Most of their rise happened between about 80 and 55 million years ago, around the time [[@extinction|the last dinosaurs lived]]. Later, during the ice ages, [[@glaciers|glaciers]] sharpened the peaks and carved deep U-shaped valleys and lakes.
Colorado alone has more than 50 peaks above 14,000 feet (about 4,270 metres). Locals call them "fourteeners", and some people spend years trying to climb every one.

st.reveal: Denali, at about 6,190 metres, belongs to the Alaska Range. The highest Rocky Mountain peak, Mount Elbert, is about 1,800 metres lower. Mount Mitchell, in the old worn-down Appalachians, is barely over 2,000 metres.
