sec.t:
As you climb the Rockies, the land changes in bands. Dry grassland gives way to pine and spruce forest, and above about 3,500 metres in Colorado the trees stop. Up there is alpine [[tundra|tundra]], a land of low flowers, lichens and wind.

Bighorn sheep, with huge curled horns, leap across ledges. Mountain goats, with white shaggy coats, live on even steeper cliffs. Elk gather in herds, and in autumn the males make a high, whistling call called bugling. Grizzly bears still roam the northern Rockies, in [[@usa-wonder-yellowstone|Yellowstone]], Glacier National Park and Canada. In Yellowstone, [[@yellowstone-wolves|wolves]] were brought back in 1995 after being wiped out decades earlier.

For travellers heading west, the Rockies were a wall. In 1805, the explorers [[@lewis-clark|Meriwether Lewis and William Clark]], guided in part by a young Shoshone woman named [[@usa-sacagawea|Sacagawea]], struggled across the Bitterroot Mountains in snow and nearly starved.

Railways came later. Canada's first railway across the country was finished in 1885, climbing through the Rockies at Kicking Horse Pass. The same year, Canada set aside land near [[@geysers-hot-springs|hot springs]] at Banff, which grew into the country's first national park. Today trains, highways and tunnels cross the range, but storms still close mountain passes in winter.

Denver, the capital of Colorado, is nicknamed the "Mile High City" because it sits about 1,600 metres above sea level. One step on the state Capitol building is marked as one mile high.

Air is thinner at that height, so there is less air pressure pushing down on the water in a pot. Water [[@boiling-water|boils]] at a lower temperature, about 95°C, and food takes longer to cook. Visitors from the coast often feel short of breath for a day or two. Athletes sometimes train in Colorado on purpose, because their bodies make extra red blood cells to cope with the thin air. In Ladakh, India's soldiers and [[@mountaineering|climbers]] know the same trick.

text: [[@what-if-earth-stopped|The Earth spins once every 24 hours]], so the Sun can't be overhead everywhere at once. When it is noon in Mumbai, it is early morning in [[@london|London]] and the middle of the night in New York.

To make clocks match the Sun's position roughly, the world is divided into time zones. Each full turn of the Earth is 360 degrees, and 360 divided by 24 hours makes 15 degrees an hour. So, in theory, every 15 degrees of longitude east, clocks go forward an hour. In practice, countries draw their zones along borders and choose what suits them, so the lines on a time-zone map zigzag a lot.

sec.h: When every town had its own time
sec.t:
For most of history, people set their [[@clocks|clocks]] by the Sun. When it was highest in the sky, it was noon. Because the Sun moves across the sky, noon in one town arrived a few minutes earlier or later than in the next town east or west.

This did not matter when travel was slow. Then came the railways, in America and later across India, as told in [[@indian-railways|India's railways]]. A train crossing a country needed a timetable that made sense. In the United States in the 1800s, railways juggled dozens of local times. On 18 November 1883, US and Canadian railways switched to a few standard time zones. People called it "the day of two noons", because many towns reset their clocks at midday.

India covers about 30 degrees of longitude, which should mean roughly two hours of Sun-time difference. Yet the whole country uses one time zone, India Standard Time, which is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of UTC. It is based on a line at 82.5 degrees east, passing near Mirzapur in Uttar Pradesh. The official time is kept by the CSIR-National Physical Laboratory in New Delhi.

Bombay and Calcutta kept their own local times for many years, and Bombay Time lasted until 1955. Today, one clock helps trains, flights and offices run smoothly across India. But in the north-east, the Sun can rise before 5 am in summer and set by around 4.30 pm in winter. [[@assam-tea|Tea gardens in Assam]] have long kept their own unofficial "tea garden time", an hour ahead, and some people argue India should have two time zones.

sec.h: The United States and its zones
sec.t:
The US mainland has four main time zones: Eastern, Central, Mountain and Pacific. Alaska and Hawaii have their own. When a family in Los Angeles sits down for breakfast at 7 am, friends in New York are already at 10 am.

Most of the US also uses daylight saving time, moving clocks forward one hour in spring and back in autumn, to give longer light evenings in summer. India does not.

If you keep going east, adding an hour every zone, you eventually have to drop a whole day. That happens at the International Date Line, in the middle of the Pacific. Cross it heading west and you jump forward to tomorrow.

The line bends around islands and countries. In 1995, the island nation of Kiribati moved the line so its whole [[territory|territory]] shared the same date. Some of its islands are now among the first places on Earth to greet each [[@new-year|new year]]. Exact time matters more than ever today: your phone's [[@gps-how|GPS]] works by comparing time signals from satellites that are accurate to billionths of a second.

text: Victoria Falls is a huge waterfall on the Zambezi River in southern Africa, on the border between Zambia and Zimbabwe. The river, almost 1.7 km wide at that point, tumbles over a cliff into a deep, narrow gorge. In some places it falls about 108 m, roughly twice the height of the main part of [[@niagara-falls|Niagara Falls]].

Because the river is so wide and the drop so deep, Victoria Falls is often described as the largest curtain of falling water on Earth. In the rainy months, the spray rises hundreds of metres into the air and can be seen from many kilometres away. That is why the local name is Mosi-oa-Tunya, the smoke that thunders.

st.reveal: The spray rises like smoke, sometimes hundreds of metres into the sky, and the roar of the water can be heard far off. The name comes from the Kololo people who lived in the area in the 1800s.

Angel Falls in Venezuela drops about 979 m, roughly nine times as far. Victoria Falls is famous because it is both very wide and high, which makes it one of the largest single sheets of falling water anywhere.

sec.t:
The falls drop into a crack. About 180 million years ago, [[lava|lava]] flooded this part of Africa and cooled into hard [[basalt|basalt]]. As it cooled, it split along long cracks, which later filled with softer material.

When the Zambezi began flowing across the basalt, it found these weak lines and scoured them out. The water falls into one crack, then escapes through a narrow gap at one end. Over a very long time, the river has eaten backwards into new cracks, abandoning old ones. The zigzag gorges below the falls are former waterfall sites, a record of how the [[@waterfalls|waterfall]] has moved upstream. [[geologist|Geologists]] count several older gorges, and at one end of today's falls the river is already cutting into the next weak line.

Above the edge, the Zambezi is wide and dotted with islands. One of them, Livingstone Island, sits right on the lip of the falls.

The amount of water changes hugely through the year. After the rainy season, around March and April, more than 500 million litres can pour over the edge every minute. Then the spray is so thick that visitors get soaked, and sometimes you can hardly see the falls at all.

By October and November, near the end of the dry season, the flow is much lower. Parts of the Zambian side can shrink to bare rock. In very dry years, such as 2019, photos of the thin falls made news around the world.

sec.h: Explorers, a bridge and brave swimmers
sec.t:
The Tonga, Lozi and other peoples living nearby knew the falls for centuries before outsiders arrived. In November 1855, the Scottish missionary David Livingstone became the first European known to see them. He named them after Britain's Queen Victoria.

In 1905, a steel arch [[@bridges|bridge]] was finished across the gorge just below the falls, carrying a railway over the Zambezi. It still links Zambia and Zimbabwe, and people now bungee jump from it.

On the Zambian side, at the very lip of the falls, is a rock pool called the Devil's Pool. In the low-water months, guides take visitors to swim in it, right at the edge of the drop. A natural rock wall under the water stops them from going over. Few swimming pools anywhere have a view like it, straight down a wall of falling water into the gorge.

text: A secret language is a way of speaking or writing that only insiders can understand. Some are simple games that twist ordinary words, like Pig Latin in English. Others are full scripts or codes, created to keep messages private from outsiders.

People make secret languages for fun, to bond with friends, to hide plans from rivals or to protect themselves. Children invent them in playgrounds everywhere. But adults have used them too, from street traders to soldiers to women in a corner of China who built an entire secret script.

sec.t:
The easiest secret languages take a normal language and scramble it with a rule. In Pig Latin, you move the first consonant sound to the end of each word and add "ay". So "secret" becomes "ecretsay". It sounds like nonsense until you crack the rule.

In the USA, a 1970s children's TV show called *Zoom* made *Ubbi Dubbi* famous. You add "ub" before each vowel sound, so "talk" becomes "tubalk". In France, young people speak *verlan*, flipping the [[syllable|syllables]] of words. The name itself comes from *l'envers*, "the reverse". Some verlan words are now so common they appear in French dictionaries. *Meuf*, verlan for *femme*, meaning woman, is one of them.

sec.h: A code no one could break
sec.t:
During the Second World War, the US Marines used a living language as a code. Navajo speakers, known as [[@code-talkers|code talkers]], sent messages by radio in Navajo, with special words for military things. A tank was called a "turtle", and a submarine an "iron fish".

The language was complex and almost unknown outside the Navajo Nation. Enemy codebreakers never cracked it. The code talkers' work stayed secret for decades. They were only honoured publicly long after the war.

Some twins develop a private way of talking as toddlers, using words only they understand. In the 1970s, twin sisters in San Diego, USA, spoke in a language so strange that experts first thought it was invented. It turned out to be a blend of English and German they had heard at home, spoken very fast and changed in their own way.

Traders in markets around the world have used private codes for prices so customers could not follow along. Travelling entertainers, actors and other groups who faced unfair treatment have used secret slangs to protect themselves. In Britain, a slang called Polari was used by performers and others in the 1900s, and some of its words slipped into everyday English.

Some secret languages are not spoken at all. In parts of Turkey, the Canary Islands and elsewhere, people talk across valleys by [[@whistled-languages|whistling]]. Others are hidden in writing, using codes and [[@cipher-codes|ciphers]] that scramble letters by a secret rule. Today, the messages on your phone are protected by a secret language of maths, called [[@encryption|encryption]], that no human could ever read by eye.

text: An egg is a package designed to grow a chick. On the outside is the shell. Just inside are two thin skins, called membranes. At the wide end is a small air pocket. Then comes the egg white, which is mostly water and [[protein|protein]], and in the middle, the yellow yolk, which is packed with fat, protein and [[@vitamins|vitamins]].

Look closely at a raw egg and you'll see twisted white cords on either side of the yolk. These are the chalazae, which hold the yolk in the middle like a hammock. Most eggs sold in shops come from hens that never met a rooster, so they are not fertilised and will never become chicks.

st.prompt: Put a very old egg in a bowl of water and it floats. Why?

The yolk dries up and becomes as light as a sponge
Old eggs grow a lighter shell

st.reveal: An egg has a small air pocket at its wide end. As days pass, moisture escapes through the tiny pores and air takes its place, so the pocket grows. Eventually the egg is buoyant enough to float. Fresh eggs sink and lie flat.

sec.t:
An eggshell is made of calcium carbonate, the same stuff as chalk and limestone. A hen needs a lot of calcium to make one, which is why farmers often give hens crushed shells or grit.

The shell is dotted with thousands of tiny pores, too small to see. In a fertilised egg, oxygen comes in and [[carbon-dioxide|carbon dioxide]] goes out through them as the chick grows. A thin coating on the outside, called the bloom, helps keep germs out. In the USA, eggs are washed before sale, which removes the bloom, so they must be kept in the fridge.

sec.h: What the white and yolk do

sec.t:
Raw egg white is clear because its proteins are curled up into tight balls. Heat makes them unravel and tangle into a firm white mesh, which is why the white turns solid and opaque.

That's also why eggs are so useful in [[@baking|baking]]. They hold cakes together, trap air when whisked, and help batters set in the oven. Whisk an egg white for a few minutes and it can swell to several times its size, into white foam called meringue.

A hen's egg is small compared with an [[@penguin-flight|ostrich]] egg, which can weigh about 1.4 kg, as much as about two dozen hen's eggs. The tiniest bird eggs, laid by some [[@hummingbirds|hummingbirds]], are smaller than a jelly bean.

Before it is fertilised, an ostrich yolk is part of a single giant egg [[@body-cells|cell]], among the biggest cells of any living animal. Bird eggs come in many colours, from the blue eggs of robins to the speckled eggs of plovers.

India is one of the world's biggest egg producers, with Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and Telangana leading. Namakkal in Tamil Nadu is so full of poultry farms that it is often called India's egg city.

Many Indian states serve boiled eggs in school [[@mid-day-meal|mid-day meals]] because they are cheap and full of protein. Other states don't, out of respect for families who are vegetarian. Egg bhurji, the spiced scrambled egg cooked on street griddles, is a late-night favourite in many cities.

text: Umami is a savoury, meaty, mouth-filling taste. It is the fifth basic taste, alongside sweet, sour, salty and bitter. You find it in ripe [[@tomatoes|tomatoes]], cheese, mushrooms, soy sauce, meat broth, dried fish and seaweed.

The taste comes mainly from glutamate, a building block of [[protein|proteins]]. When proteins break down, through ripening, cooking, drying or fermenting, glutamate is set free, and special [[sensor|sensors]] on your [[@tongue-taste|tongue]] pick it up. Umami tells your brain that a food probably contains protein, something your body needs. Sweet signals energy, salty signals minerals, and bitter often warns of poison, so each taste works like a quick lab test done in your mouth.

sec.t:
Kikunae Ikeda was a chemistry professor in Tokyo. His wife made dashi, a clear Japanese broth from kombu [[@seaweed-food|seaweed]]. Ikeda noticed it had a taste that was not sweet, sour, salty or bitter. In 1908 he boiled down huge amounts of kombu, crystallised the substance behind the taste and found it was glutamate.

He called the taste umami. The very next year, a company began selling his seasoning, a salt form of glutamate called monosodium glutamate, or MSG. Ikeda hoped it would make cheap, plain food tastier for poor families.

Later, Japanese researchers found something odd. Two other substances, one in dried bonito fish and one in dried shiitake mushrooms, have only a little taste alone. Mixed with glutamate, they make umami many times stronger.

Cooks had used this trick for centuries without knowing why. Food scientists today call it umami synergy, and snack makers use it on purpose, which is one reason a packet of chips can be so hard to stop eating. Dashi combines kombu and bonito. Italians put parmesan on tomato sauce. A burger with ketchup, cheese and meat stacks several umami foods together.

Indian cooking is full of umami, even if nobody uses the word. Onions and tomatoes slowly fried into a masala become richer as they brown. Dried fish is loved along the Konkan coast and in the Northeast. In Nagaland, a fermented soybean paste called axone has a strong, savoury smell that fills a whole kitchen. [[@fermentation|Fermentation]] of rice and dal for idli and dosa batter also releases glutamate.

In the USA, ketchup, parmesan, mushrooms and slow-cooked barbecue all lean on umami. Even the ancient Romans loved it: they poured a salty fermented fish sauce called garum on almost everything.

In 1968, a doctor wrote a letter to a medical journal describing feeling unwell after meals at Chinese restaurants in the USA. Newspapers blamed MSG, and the idea of "Chinese restaurant syndrome" spread, along with unfair suspicion of Chinese food.

Since then, many careful studies, where people did not know if they were eating MSG, have found no reliable harm from normal amounts. A ripe tomato or a piece of parmesan contains the very same glutamate. But taste is never just the tongue. Hold your nose and much of a food's flavour disappears, because your [[@taste-smell-link|sense of smell]] does more of the tasting than you think.
